say: You give it a quadratic trinomial, $ax^2 + bx + c$. It writes it as a product of two **brackets**.
The key idea: split the middle term into two pieces whose numbers multiply to $a \times c$ and add to $b$. Then the brackets pull out.

how.higher: Higher level uses it as a step inside bigger questions, mostly Paper 1: solving a cubic once one factor is known, or finding where a graph crosses the axis.
how.ordinary: Ordinary level asks for it directly on Paper 1, either as a short part of its own worth 10 marks, or as the step that solves a quadratic equation.

steps.title: Find the two numbers
steps.say: Multiply the first and last numbers: $2 \times 10 = 20$. Look for two numbers that multiply to $\hl{1}{20}$ and add to $\hl{2}{9}$.

steps.title: Split the middle term
steps.say: Write the $9x$ as $4x + 5x$. The value of the expression does not change.

steps.title: Take out common factors
steps.say: Pair the terms. Take the common factor out of each pair. Both pairs now leave the same bracket.

steps.title: Take out the bracket
steps.say: The bracket $(x+2)$ is common to both parts. Take it out, and what is left forms the other bracket.

lines.text: Check by multiplying out: you get $2x^2 + 9x + 10$ back.

higher.tip: When you know one root, divide it out and finish the division. A full division with no remainder earns marks on its own.
Once the cubic is reduced to a quadratic, you may factorise it or use the formula. Both are accepted, so use whichever you trust.
Partial credit goes for correct division even if you do not finish, so always set the division up and show it.

sources.quote: some correct division, or sets up long division correctly

ordinary.tip: Move every term to one side so it equals $0$ before you factorise. That rearranging is a step the marks are tied to.
A quadratic gives two answers. If one does not fit the story, say which you keep and why.
Even one correct factor of the constant earns marks, so write down the factor pairs.
Marks are given for the factorised form on its own, so write the brackets out before solving.

say: You give it a diagram with an unknown angle on a circle. It finds the angle and **names the theorem** that justifies it.
Theorem 19: the angle at the **centre** is twice the angle at the circle, when both stand on the same arc.
what.in: circle with two angles on one arc

how.higher: Higher level has used it in a proof on Paper 2 (2022, a 5-mark part), where the proof is built from the angle at the centre being twice the angle at the circle.

example.question: $A$, $B$ and $C$ are points on a circle with centre $O$. The angle at the centre is $|\angle AOB| = (6x - 10)^\circ$ and the angle at the circle is $|\angle ACB| = (2x + 5)^\circ$. Both stand on the arc $AB$. Find $x$ and $|\angle ACB|$.

steps.title: Name the two angles
steps.say: Both angles stand on the same arc $AB$. $\hl{1}{|\angle AOB|}$ is at the centre. $\hl{2}{|\angle ACB|}$ is at the circle.

steps.title: Apply Theorem 19
steps.say: By Theorem 19, the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circle. So $\hl{1}{|\angle AOB|} = 2\hl{2}{|\angle ACB|}$.

steps.title: Solve for x
steps.say: Multiply out the bracket, then collect the $x$ terms on one side.

steps.title: Find the angle at the circle
steps.say: Substitute $x = 10$ into the angle at the circle.

say: You give it a line $l$ and a point $P$ on it. It draws the line through $P$ that meets $l$ at a **right angle**.
The key idea: mark two points the same distance either side of $P$. Any point the same distance from both of them lies on the perpendicular.

how.higher: It appeared on Paper 2 in 2016 as a 5-mark construction part, where the perpendicular was one stage of a longer construction.

example.question: Draw a line $l$ and mark a point $P$ on it. Construct the line through $P$ perpendicular to $l$.

steps.title: Mark equal distances
steps.say: Put the compass point on $P$. Draw an arc that cuts $l$ on each side of $P$. Call the points $A$ and $B$.

lines.text: Keep the compass setting the same for both arcs, so $|PA| = |PB|$.

steps.title: Open the compass wider
steps.say: Open the compass wider than $|PA|$. With the point on $A$, draw an arc above the line.

lines.text: Do not change the setting yet.

steps.title: Cross the arcs
steps.say: Keep the same setting. With the point on $B$, draw an arc that crosses the first one. Call the crossing $Q$.

lines.text: Leave all arcs on the page. They are the construction lines.

steps.title: Join the points
steps.say: With the ruler, draw a straight line from $P$ through $Q$.

say: You give it a formula for a sum, $\Sigma$, that you are told is true for every $n$. It **proves** it in three moves.
Show it works for $n = 1$. Assume it works for $n = k$. Then use that to show it works for $n = k + 1$.

how.higher: Higher level asks for it on Paper 1, usually as a 15-mark part at the end of a question (2020 and 2025), where the sum or formula is given and you prove it.

example.question: Prove by induction that $1 + 3 + 5 + \cdots + (2n - 1) = n^2$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

steps.title: Check n = 1
steps.say: Test the formula for $n = 1$. The sum has one term.

lines.text: They match, so it is true for $n = 1$.

steps.title: Assume true for k
steps.say: Assume the formula is true for $n = k$. This is what you will use.

steps.title: Prove for k + 1
steps.say: Now take $n = k + 1$. Add the next term, $2k + 1$, to the sum for $k$. Replace the sum for $k$ with $k^2$.

lines.text: To prove: the sum to $k+1$ terms is $(k + 1)^2$.

steps.title: Write the conclusion
steps.say: State all three parts of the conclusion. It is a step the marks are tied to.

lines.text: True for $n = 1$. If true for $n = k$, then true for $n = k + 1$. So true for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

higher.tip: Finish with a concluding statement. Leaving it out costs a mark.
The conclusion has three parts: true for the first case, true for $k$ implies true for $k+1$, and so true for all $n$. Write all three.
The base case and the assumption can come in either order, so do not worry about the order.
